text.p: The terms monetarism and monetarists have been used in this pre-election campaign, sometimes in a confusing and misleading way. Following is a brief description of this school of economic thought.
As respected Keynesian and Nobel laureate Franco Mondigliani put it: "We are all monetarists now." At least partly.
Monetarism favours a small public sector, minimal government interference in the economy, abhors budget deficits and public debt.

Monetarism believes that fine-tuning of the economy leads to greater real output variation than sticking to a fixed monetary policy rule (K-percent money supply rule) and letting the private sector function freely.
The label monetarism was coined by the late Karl Brunner, a monetarist to describe Milton Friedman's views. Nobel laureate Milton Friedman is the most famous modern proponent of monetarism.
The quantity theory of money is at the centre of monetarist theory.

Major contributors in the quantity theory of money have been French philosopher Jean Bodin in the early 17th century, Scottish philosopher and economist David Hume - a close friend of Adam Smith - British economist Henry Thornton and U.S economist Irving Fisher.
QUANTITY THEORY OF MONEY: M*V = P*Y
where M: money stock
V: Velocity of money
P: Price level
Y real output

According to Friedman's restatement of the theory: Variations in the money supply can produce short-run, temporary variations in real output but changes in the money supply are fully reflected in the price level in the long-run given the long-run stability of the velocity of money and real output being fixed at the full employment level.
K-PERCENT RULE: let the money supply grow at a steady rate equal to the average GDP growth rate.
Scope for countercyclical policies remains in the short-run because labour unions exhibit adaptive expectations in wage negotiations.
ADAPTIVE EXPECTATIONS: Economic agents adapt their expectations in the light of past experience and learn from their mistakes.
expP(t+1) = expP(t) + a*( P(t)-expP(t) where 0a1
expP(t+1) : expected price level at time (t+1)
expP(t) : expected price level at time (t)
P(t) : actual price level at time (t)
a : coefficient
The restriction placed on the coefficient (a) implies that the influence of past expectations wanes geometrically with the passage of time.

FOREIGN EXCHANGE POLICY: Monetarists advocate a freely floating foreign exchange mechanism. They do not favour dirty float or pegged foreign exchange systems. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
